description: ICS Village at DEF CON 25 covers Industrial Control Systems security and critical infrastructure protection. The talks explore Modbus vulnerabilities, industrial wireless security, grid insecurity, DFIR for ICS, device-level security, and building automation security.

talks.title: Fun with Modbus 0x5a: Nothing New, Still Relevant?
talks.teaser: Historical analysis of Modbus protocol vulnerabilities and their continued relevance to modern ICS systems.
talks.summary:
### The Reality of Industrial Control System "Forever-Days"
At 00:00, Arnaud Soullié introduces the concept of industrial control "forever-days"—vulnerabilities that exist not because of complex zero-day exploitation, but due to intentional legacy design choices in Operational Technology (OT) protocols. While IT networks prioritize confidentiality and patch management, industrial networks historically prioritized operational reliability and uptime, deploying plain-text supervisory protocols without native authentication or encryption.

### Deconstructing Modbus Protocol Mechanics
At 04:10, Soullié explains the architecture of the Modbus protocol, the venerable industrial messaging standard operating on TCP port 502. He notes that while standard function codes (such as `0x01` for reading coils or `0x03` for reading holding registers) are well-documented for routine telemetry polling, PLC vendors frequently implement proprietary, undocumented function codes to execute advanced administrative actions over the same open transport layer.

### Modicon PLCs and Undocumented Function Code 0x5a
At 08:15 and 12:06, the presentation examines Schneider Electric Modicon PLCs (including the M340, Premium, and Quantum platforms). Soullié reveals how these controllers implement function code `0x5a` (UMAS - Unified Messaging Application Services). Using custom Python scripts, he demonstrates communicating directly with the PLC via `0x5a` to execute complete administrative takeovers without requiring passwords or cryptographic handshakes: reading raw memory blocks, stopping and starting the PLC CPU, and uploading or downloading compiled ladder logic programs.

### Live Logic Tampering and Process Subversion
At 15:40 and 18:25, Soullié conducts live demonstrations against target PLCs. He shows how an attacker on the control network can inject UMAS commands to extract the running project directly from the controller to a PC, inject modified ladder logic into memory, and resume CPU execution. This allows an adversary to falsify physical process behaviors—such as opening valves or disabling safety trips—while transmitting fabricated sensor data back to human operators on the HMI.

### Defensive Countermeasures and OT Network Segmentation
Concluding between 20:30 and 22:45, Soullié explores mitigation strategies for securing legacy OT environments. Because legacy controllers cannot be patched to support cryptographic authentication without complete hardware replacements, asset owners must enforce rigorous Purdue Model network segmentation. He advocates deploying deep packet inspection (DPI) industrial firewalls configured to block unauthorized Modbus function codes—specifically filtering `0x5a` from reaching critical field controllers.

talks.title: Grid Insecurity and How to Really Fix This
talks.teaser: Critical vulnerabilities in electrical grid infrastructure and practical solutions for improving security and resilience.
talks.summary:
### Demystifying Electric Grid Cybersecurity
At 00:00, Bryson Bort and Atlas open with a provocative reality check on the electrical grid: cybersecurity discussions in the energy sector are frequently dominated by sensationalized fear, uncertainty, and doubt (FUD). Mainstream narratives often depict grid takedowns as requiring well-funded, military-grade nation-state actors. In reality, the authors argue, basic system misconfigurations, unpatched industrial components, and weak perimeter boundaries leave energy infrastructure vulnerable to far less sophisticated adversaries.

### The True Attack Surface: Legacy SCADA and IT/OT Convergence
At 06:40 and 11:15, the speakers survey the actual technical terrain of electrical utilities. They emphasize that while power generation facilities and transmission sub-stations employ robust physical safety interlocks, the IT/OT convergence over the past decade has interconnected corporate enterprise networks with legacy Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) systems. Remote management interfaces, cellular modems on remote terminal units (RTUs), and unsegmented vendor maintenance links expose critical switching equipment directly to external exploitation.

### Economic Misalignments and the Regulatory Quagmire
At 15:17 and 20:45, the presentation dives into the financial and regulatory structural obstacles crippling grid defense. Electrical utilities operate under rigid state utility commission rate-recovery models where capital investments are subsidized, but cybersecurity operational expenditures are heavily scrutinized. Furthermore, mandatory compliance frameworks like NERC CIP create a check-box mentality where organizations spend millions auditing perimeter documentation rather than implementing resilient engineering defenses.

### Active Defense and Threat Emulation
At 25:10, Bort introduces the concept of active defense and automated threat emulation within industrial environments. He explains that waiting for passive intrusion detection alerts is insufficient; security teams must safely emulate adversary tactics (such as living-off-the-land techniques and unauthorized protocol polling) to validate whether internal detection pipelines and segmentation firewalls successfully isolate unauthorized lateral movement between corporate IT and field operations.

### Practical Steps for Real-World Grid Resilience
Concluding from 28:00 to 30:30, the speakers outline practical remediation strategies for asset owners. They advocate abandoning pure compliance checklists in favor of consequence-driven cyber-informed engineering (CCE). By isolating safety systems, deploying out-of-band monitoring, and ensuring manual physical fallback capabilities during grid upsets, utilities can maintain power delivery even when cyber boundaries are breached.

talks.title: Cyber Security Issues with Level 0 through 1 Devices
talks.teaser: Security vulnerabilities and threats affecting the lowest levels of industrial control device hierarchies.
talks.summary:
### The Blind Spot of Industrial Cybersecurity: Level 0 and 1
At 00:00, veteran industrial safety expert Joe Weiss opens with a critique of modern operational technology (OT) cybersecurity: industry frameworks (such as NERC CIP and IEC 62443) concentrate almost exclusively on Level 2 and above—human-machine interfaces (HMIs), engineering workstations, and network switches. Meanwhile, Level 0 devices (process sensors, transmitters, flow meters) and Level 1 devices (controllers, actuators, variable frequency drives) are virtually ignored, despite being the physical actuators and sensory organs of the physical plant.

### Unauthenticated Field Signaling and Analog Insecurities
At 07:15 and 12:40, Weiss explains that field instruments communicate via legacy 4-20mA current loops, HART, Modbus, and Foundation Fieldbus protocols that lack cryptographic authentication, encryption, or integrity checks. Sensors assume that any electrical signal received is valid. Consequently, an adversary who tampers with a field instrument or injects malicious signaling can spoof temperature or pressure readings, blinding control algorithms without generating network-level alarms.

### Catastrophic Case Studies: Stuxnet, Aurora, and Ukrainian Grid Outages
At 18:15 and 24:30, the presentation examines high-profile industrial incidents to demonstrate the fatal consequences of compromised sensor data. Weiss revisits Stuxnet, showing that the malware succeeded not simply by modifying PLC code, but by recording legitimate sensor values and replaying them back to operators while centrifuges were destroyed. He also discusses the Aurora Generator Test and the 2014 Ukrainian electrical grid intrusions, highlighting how malware and unauthorized commands exploit trusted sensor inputs to induce irreversible physical equipment damage.

### The Flawed Assumption of Sensor Trustworthiness
At 28:50, Weiss challenges the foundational assumption underpinning all process safety: that sensor data presented to operators and safety instrumented systems (SIS) is inherently trustworthy. He illustrates how mechanical engineers, process operators, and corporate cybersecurity teams remain siloed, preventing organizations from diagnosing whether an abnormal physical reading is caused by mechanical failure, maintenance error, or deliberate cyber tampering.

### Real-Time Instrumentation Monitoring and Future Defenses
Concluding between 32:10 and 35:06, Weiss calls for immediate technological intervention at the instrumentation level. He emphasizes that monitoring IP packets at switch spans is insufficient; industrial facilities must deploy dedicated, physics-based instrumentation monitoring appliances that sample raw electrical waveforms directly at the sensor wire level. By comparing high-frequency physical dynamics against reported digital values, operators can detect sensor spoofing and prevent equipment destruction in real time.
